lithuania:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Grand Duchy of Lithuania holds the forests, bogs and lake country between the Neman and Neris rivers. The settlement that later grew into Vilnius lies near the meeting of the Vilnia and Neris, but its form and defenses in 1259 are uncertain. Trakai's island castle belongs to the fourteenth century and should not be treated as Mindaugas's residence or treasury. Few realms in Europe enjoy such deep natural defenses. Dense primeval woodland covers most of the land, and marsh belts swallow heavy horses whole. Good farmland is small and scattered along a few river valleys, so most grain comes from slash-and-burn clearings in the forest. The forest gives the country its exports: shipbuilding oak and pine, winter furs, wild honey and beeswax. These goods float down the Neman, where they are traded for salt and iron from the south. No firm overland road links Vilnius to the Baltic, so the realm's foreign trade depends on a few waterways.

Legitimacy and the crown. Grand Duke Mindaugas cleared his rivals with ruthless force. Around 1251 he accepted Roman baptism, and in 1253 he received a royal crown through papal envoys, which gave the Lithuanian state a standing in the Latin world. Beneath that parchment, however, many subjects and tribal elders still honor the old Baltic gods, Perkunas the thunder god and Zemyna the earth mother. Sacred oaks, altars and eternal fires remain in use in the forests. The duke swears Latin oaths in Vilnius and then offers prayers in the local tongue at the sacred groves. His aims are to push the frontier to the Neman and the upper Bug, to win Western recognition of his rule over Samogitia and the Rus borderlands, and to make the crown hereditary in his own line rather than leave succession to the council of elders.

Taxation and the war economy. The treasury does not rest on manorial rent. Its first income is tribute from the Slavic settlements to the east, collected each autumn by the duke's riders in grain, cattle and coarse cloth. Villages that fail to pay are burned, and young men are taken off to forest labor. The second source is the fur monopoly. Hunters must sell the best marten and bear pelts to court buying stations at fixed prices, and anyone who sells privately loses the whole catch. The third is captives. Most are sold to Rus merchants in exchange for salt, iron and cloth. Local elders keep part of the tribute, but they must account to the duke's clerks at the winter assembly. The system works only while raids continue, and a quiet frontier leaves the court short of coin.

Military system. The army has two main parts. Noble cavalry wear mail and carry light shields. They charge and pursue on short steppe horses that have stamina but cannot carry heavy armor for long. Forest infantry come from the clans. Young men carry javelins, short bows and long-handled axes, train in the hunting grounds and set out on campaign with only three to five days of food. The duke's household guard numbers a few hundred young baptized knights who rotate duty at Vilnius castle. Tactics favor ambush at river crossings and marsh edges. Light horse lure heavy knights into soft ground, and then javelin men and infantry close from both flanks. The army has few siege engines. Against the brick castles of the Teutonic Knights it can only surround a fortress, burn the outlying villages and hope to draw the garrison into a field battle.

Geopolitical crisis. The Livonian Order of the Sword in the north and the Teutonic Order in the west press on the Samogitian lands like two iron pincers. Each new stone castle on the forest edge becomes a base for raids into Lithuanian territory, and the knights are building a chain of fortified points to cut the forest road to the Baltic coast. To the east, Polotsk and Smolensk watch every Lithuanian move toward Slavic land, and several small Smolensk border forts have already fallen in night raids. To the south, Turov and Pinsk compete with Lithuania for river crossings and salt routes through the marsh country. The Neman and Neris waterways are the realm's lifeline. If the Order cuts the Samogitian corridor, Vilnius loses its route to the Baltic and its only path for reinforcements from the west.

Internal factions. Mindaugas and Treniota should not be described as openly divided in 1259. Later accounts connect Treniota's influence over policy and Lithuania's turn against the Order to the aftermath of the 1260 Battle of Durbe. For 1259, describe disagreement over baptism and alliances as a latent court tension, not an established break. Mindaugas relies on his newly baptized knights and on Vilnius merchants, and he buys the loyalty of several clans by granting them forest estates. The court itself is split. One faction wants to keep working with the papacy to win a truce from the Order. Another wants to restore ties with the Orthodox princes of Novgorod and Kyiv to counterbalance the West. Northern pressure and religious disagreement require the duke to balance cooperation with the papacy, border defense and ties with Orthodox neighbors. Tensions over succession, baptized nobles and traditional authority remain unresolved at court.
teutonic_order:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Teutonic Order State stretches across the lower Vistula, the Kulm lands and the Baltic coastal lowlands. The land is flat and low, and rivers, lagoons and meadows cover much of it. In 1259 its Prussian strongholds included places such as Kulm, Elbing and Balga along the lower Vistula and lagoon routes. Marienburg (Malbork) had not yet been built; construction began later in the century, and the Order's headquarters moved there in 1309. The Order owns the Vistula ferries and wooden bridges, and it levies a bridge toll on boats by tonnage. Winter ice forces the crossing bridges to be dismantled before the thaw and rebuilt afterward. German grain, cloth, iron and wine arrive by sea and move upriver on the Vistula. Coastal fisheries and salt pans supply the convents, and the amber trade pays for the castle garrisons and the craftsmen who serve them.

Legitimacy and the crown. The Order holds papal privileges and the recognition of the Holy Roman Emperor. These grant it the right to conquer pagan land and to bring it into the Church. Grand Master Anno von Sangerhausen, who has led the Order since 1256, directs the brothers through its commanderies and presents the Order as the servant of the Virgin Mary. Its courts govern new land under the Kulm law. Baptized peasants may hold land and town rights, while unbaptized Prussians become serfs bound to their manors. Judgments carry the Grand Master's seal and are copied to the bishop of Kulm for record. The Order's central aim is to take all of Prussia and western Lithuania, to become the only religious and political power in the eastern Baltic, and to keep the office of Grand Master in the hands of German knights rather than local bishops or imperial princes.

Taxation and the war economy. Revenue is more orderly than in most eastern states. Conquered Prussians owe a tithe in rye and oats. The grain is stored in Elbing and other river strongholds and converted to silver at fixed rates. The Order holds the amber trade on the Baltic coast and runs its own fleet, which carries amber to Lubeck and Bruges and returns with silver and woolen cloth. At the Vistula mouth it collects customs and warehouse fees on Hanseatic ships, and it levies consumption taxes on salt and beer. The brothers' pay and the horse fodder come straight from the stores. German crusader guests who join each campaign settle their travel costs and wages through the Order's accounts, and the number of guests is set again every year. When rebels burn the granaries, the Order borrows from Hanseatic moneylenders at high interest, and its finances quickly fall out of balance.

Military system. The army is built around heavy cavalry. Black-cross knights wear mail and early breastplates, and they attack in a wedge that can split an infantry line. Their squires ride lighter horses to carry lances, spare mounts and equipment, and they pursue broken enemies after the charge. The Order also brings siege engines, stone-throwing machines, crossbow engines and engineers who can take apart timber forts. Manpower is its weakness. Few local men become knights, so most of the army consists of German crusaders who come for a season and then go home. Mustering takes weeks. Spring thaw and autumn rain turn the roads into mud, and heavy horses sink to the girth. The Order lays timber and stone roads on the main routes and places crossbowmen and pikemen on the flanks of the cavalry, so that a mud-bound charge does not dissolve into a rout.

Geopolitical crisis. In 1259 the Order still faced local resistance, raids and unsettled control along the Prussian frontier; the Great Prussian Uprising had not yet begun. The rising that followed the 1260 Battle of Durbe must not be presented as current. Border settlements and routes remained vulnerable during campaigns and tribute collection, forcing the Order to spread garrisons along its supply lines. In the north, Lithuanian forest riders cross the Neman each year to burn the Order's border estates and carry off serfs. In the east, the Orthodox republic of Novgorod stands in open holy-war hostility to the Order. The Livonian province is equally stretched. The Order must divide limited forces among its existing strongholds, supply routes and further expansion. In 1259 the frontier situation is still marked by scattered resistance, raids and unsettled control.

Internal factions. The brothers argue over supplies and the right to station troops. The Livonian province accuses the headquarters of keeping the best grain and recruits for Prussia, and it demands a larger share of the spoils. Older knights want an alliance with the Pomeranian dukes to secure the northern sea road. Younger knights favor crushing Prussia at any cost and building more castles. The priest brothers want the knights' privileges reduced and their property moved into the convents. Prussian villagers may answer burdensome service and dues through flight, refusal or local raids; whether those grievances will unite across clans depends on later events. The Order's current stability depends on whether the Grand Master can keep these factions in balance.
novgorod:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Republic of Novgorod spans the cold northern forest belt of northwestern Rus, the Volkhov river basin and the Lake Ladoga waterways, and its lands run north to the White Sea and west toward the Urals. The city sits on both banks of the Volkhov. St Sophia's Cathedral stands on the western bank and serves as the spiritual center, and the great bell in its tower calls the citizens to the assembly. The Yaroslav court is across the river, where government offices and the courts meet. Rapids and wooden bridges often hamper traffic on the Volkhov, so cargo is unloaded at the quays along the bends. The climate is harsh, the bogs are wide and local fields yield little grain. Bread therefore comes mostly from the black earth plains of Vladimir and Suzdal to the south, which leaves the city's food supply exposed to any blockade.

Legitimacy and the crown. Novgorod is the only republic in Rus governed by an assembly of nobles and citizens. Supreme authority belongs to the Veche, which gathers in the market square after the bell is rung. Its districts send delegates who sit in separate groups. The knyaz is not hereditary. He is a military commander and judge whom the Veche hires under a written contract that fixes his term, his pay and the ban on private estates outside the city. Princes, boyars and citizens all swear to observe the city's statutes before the icon in St Sophia. The archbishop may advise the assembly, but he cannot set policy alone. The republic's central aims are to keep its self-rule, to block the grand princes of Vladimir and the Swedes from gaining a foothold in its trade and politics, and to hold its monopoly over the northern fur and silver trade.

Taxation and the trade economy. The treasury depends on long-distance commerce. Novgorod merchants move sable furs from Siberia and the Arctic, walrus ivory, beeswax and iron through the Hanseatic counting house at Peterhof, where the goods are sold to western buyers for silver bars and fine woolen cloth. The city charges duties on incoming and outgoing goods. Every sale must be weighed by an official weigher named by the city, and the weighing fee is collected at each transaction. Districts pay a share of their tax to the Veche, which uses the money to repair the city walls, maintain the bridges and pay the mercenaries. Ships using the quays pay a mooring fee, and the owners share the cost of repairing the timber piers. When grain runs short, the city opens public granaries and sells bread at low prices. Bread prices directly shape the Veche's standing with ordinary citizens. If trade stops, tax revenue falls quickly and the city's expenses become hard to meet.

Military system. The army rests on a citizen militia. Every district raises men by household, and each recruit brings his own spear, shield or bow and takes turns guarding the walls and the quays. The heavy troops are the boyars' cavalry, who wear mail and carry sabers and are paid from the city purse. The Novgorod method is defensive counterattack. Men build floating barriers and palisades on the river to stop enemy horsemen. Crossbowmen stand behind large shield walls and fire into an advancing enemy, and spearmen come forward only when the enemy line is disordered. In winter the frozen rivers become roads, and sledges and ice paths let raiders strike at enemy camps near the border. The republic has little capacity for long campaigns in open country, and its expeditions usually follow the rivers, where supply can be maintained. A distant campaign that leaves the rivers is rarely attempted.

Geopolitical crisis. The threats are serious. From the west the Swedes watch the mouth of the Neva and want the waterway to the Baltic, where they have begun to build wooden and stone outposts. The Teutonic Order works to cut Pskov away from Novgorod and bring it under its own influence, and Order merchants and agents are already moving in and out of Pskov. Grain supplies from the south depend on river seasons and Novgorod's relations with the Rus principalities. Pressure from the grand prince of Vladimir and the Mongol court forces the republic to weigh princely appointments, tribute and self-rule. The northern climate prevents the republic from growing enough food, so trade is its lifeline. If the sea and river routes are cut, bread prices and tax revenue collapse together, and quarrels between merchants and citizens become much more dangerous.

Internal factions. A small group of wealthy boyar families controls the storehouses, the ships and the vote-buying network, while artisans and dockworkers depend on wages that fall when trade slows. When the bell sounds, the poor gather in the square to demand lower taxes and the punishment of the oligarchs. The Veche often slides into street brawls and mob violence, and it can spend several days without reaching a decision. The prince's retinue and the citizen militia distrust each other. The militia fears that the retinue will entrench itself inside the walls, and the retinue complains that the Veche does not pay its wages on time. If an outside army reaches the walls while the factions are at war, the Veche may refuse to call up the militia, and the city's defense could collapse at the critical moment.
kyiv:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Grand Duchy of Kyiv lies along the middle Dnieper, in the black soil belt that gives Rus its richest farmland. Meadows and forests alternate along the river, and crossings and landings at the bends make Kyiv the hub where land and water routes meet. The city's golden gate, the St Sophia Cathedral and the caves of the Pechersk monastery once made it the most splendid building complex in eastern Europe. Batu's sack of 1240 left most walls and churches in ruins, and the monastery cloisters now stand broken above the river. Many outlying villages lie empty, and only the stretches of riverbank still produce wheat and barley. Fish weirs and salt landings on the river feed the town, but much of the profit goes to the Mongol tax agents and to passing merchants. On the steppe edge, earthen ramparts run across the open ground, and in summer the herds of nomad horsemen move through the valleys, so the garrison must light beacons every night.

Legitimacy and the crown. Kyiv keeps a religious and dynastic authority that no other Rus city can replace. The Orthodox metropolitan resides there, and the cathedral bells call the faithful of every principality. Alexander Yaroslavich Nevsky holds grand-princely titles associated with both Kyiv and Vladimir, but his court resides in the north. Kyiv remains under Mongol overlordship, and local administration and tribute collection should not be described as powers he personally exercises from the city. The position is contradictory. He must act as the khan's vassal to reassure the steppe envoys, and at the same time he must preserve the Rurikid dignity before the bishops and the townsfolk. His core aims are to uphold Kyiv's seniority, to make the other princes accept him as the supreme ruler of all Rus, and to use the bishops' support to keep that title legitimate in the eyes of the Church. He also wants to use his seniority to mediate between the principalities and stop them from fighting one another.

Taxation and tribute. The treasury is squeezed by the Mongol poll tax, known as the dan, and by the tolls on merchant traffic. Each household pays in silver, pelts or grain. Tax officers travel with the embassies from town to town, counting people and checking account books each year. Caravans pay customs at the river crossings, and salt, honey and fur sales are taxed. Any goods held back from the collectors are seized. Most of the silver and marten pelts collected are sent to the Saray camp on the Volga, and little money stays in the region for rebuilding. The prince's court can rely only on small judicial fines and church donations for daily expenses. Many craftsmen cannot repair their houses, and potters and blacksmiths close their workshops one by one, which speeds the town's decline.

Military system. Alexander's army combines the infantry spear wall of the Slavs with the mounted archery of the boyar bodyguard, the druzhina. The bodyguard horsemen wear mail and carry composite bows. They use lakes, marshes and the wind to draw enemies into ambush. The spearmen form shield squares to hold the city gates and river crossings. Alexander is known for winter operations in snow and open country. He can envelop the enemy's flank with mixed forces, split the enemy into pieces and destroy each part in turn. The army also depends on townsmen and peasant laborers, who cut timber and haul stone in winter to repair the gate towers. Still, the number of full-time professional troops is small. Against a punitive Golden Horde campaign, Kyiv could only delay the enemy behind its walls and marshes. It could not hope to win a pitched field battle against Mongol horse archers.

Geopolitical crisis. The steppe raiders can cross the open plain to the south at any time and sweep over the Dnieper to burn riverside villages and carry off women and children. The Galician-Volhynian kingdom to the west has its eye on the southern lands of Kyiv, and its border fortresses have been moving east step by step. Small clashes over villages in the Volhynian borderland are common. In the north, the young princes of Tver and Suzdal resent Kyiv's seniority. They keep up a show of obedience but work behind the scenes to win the tribute and the yarlyk for themselves. The borders are open on every side, and a single lapse in watch could let steppe horsemen or a neighbor's army cross the plain and reach the city.

Internal factions. The main internal conflict is between the prince's harsh collection of Mongol taxes and the armed resistance of townspeople who refuse to pay. Local artisans and townsmen have revolted over the poll tax several times, and in some towns they killed the Mongol tax officers. The prince must suppress these risings to prove his loyalty to the khan, but each suppression adds to the resentment, and some boyars quietly support the townsmen. Within the Church and the boyar class, some argue for a united front with the townsmen against the tax, while others argue that submission to the khan is the only way to keep the city's religious standing. Any attack on a tax collector could bring a second catastrophe to the whole principality.
halych_volhynia:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia occupies the wooded hills and basins north of the Carpathians, between the Dniester and the upper Western Bug. Its three main places are the old capital Halych, built on high cliffs above the Dniester gorge, the Kholm fortress that guards the forest road to Lublin, and the newer city of Lviv at the junction of trade routes. Rye, barley and good horses cover the fields. Rock salt and brine springs lie in the hills, and salt boilers work in the valleys with iron pans over open fires. Goods from the Danube lands pass through the kingdom, and furs and copper from the east pay customs at the gates. The Volhynian forests also produce beeswax and quality timber, which travel down the Western Bug toward the markets of Warsaw.

Legitimacy and the crown. Prince Danylo Romanovych is the most capable ruler in the region. In 1253 a papal legate crowned him at Dorohychyn, and he became the first ruler of Rus to hold a royal title, Rex Russiae. This gave his claim to the southwestern Rus lands a Western legal basis. The promised papal crusade against the Mongols, however, never arrived. Danylo must now deal with the Catholic West and the Mongol Khanate at the same time. He sends homage to Rome and tribute to the Mongol camps, and both sides receive his envoys with polite words and few concrete promises. His central aims are to keep the crown legitimate, to win Western troops for his frontier, and to make his kingdom the leading power among the southwestern Rus principalities.

Taxation and the salt economy. The kingdom's revenue rests on a royal monopoly on rock salt. Salt is taxed by the bag. Clerks weigh it in the town granaries, and merchants must pay before they can take their load. The state also taxes grain exported down the Danube, and grain merchants register their quantities before loading at the river ports. Caravans crossing Central Europe pay tolls by vehicle, animal and goods, and customs posts stand at the main fords. Most of the money goes straight to the royal treasury, where it pays the court, the knights and the castle repairs. Boyar lords often keep part of the salt revenue for themselves, and they exempt their peasants from some taxes in the name of their estates. The real income is therefore well below the figures written in the royal ledgers.

Military system. The kingdom has adopted the Western knightly model in full. Its heavy cavalry wear full mail and early plate, and they ride tall horses bought in Hungary and Poland. Each fief owes a set number of retainers to the crown. Light cavalry with composite bows, drawn mainly from the Slavic clans, scout and screen the army. They tend herds in the forests and valleys, and in peacetime they serve as hunters and couriers. Galicia was among the first lands of eastern Europe to build stone walls, and the walls of Halych and Kholm can withstand siege engines. The garrisons rely on crossbowmen and spearmen. Still, this force is weak against a large Mongol army of the kind led by Burundai. Two years ago Mongol commanders ordered the kingdom to pull down and burn its new stone walls and fortresses. Many masons left, and the walls remain unrepaired. Timber forts are now being built instead.

Geopolitical crisis. The danger is immediate. Mongol cavalry could cross the frontier at any time for a punitive raid, and their scouts have already been seen in the border forests. To the west, Poland and to the south, Hungary watch the frontier with papal approval and seek to seize land. Polish knights have raided villages along the Volhynian border, and Hungarian envoys have demanded tolls at the Carpathian passes. To the north, Lithuanian riders occasionally cross the Bug, and farmers in Volhynia will not clear fields along the forest edge. Each border lord keeps a record of where the Mongols crossed last time, because the next raid will probably follow the same roads. The kingdom faces enemies on three sides, so every fortress must be kept manned, and the loss of any single one could break the line.

Internal factions. The boyar magnates have long resisted the centralizing policy of the crown. They keep private armies, withhold taxes and trade information with foreign courts. Their resistance weakens the army's ability to face the next steppe campaign. The royal council is divided between those who would buy peace from the Khan and those who would defend the frontier by force. Several magnates have sent their sons to the Hungarian court as hostages, so the king cannot count on their loyalty when the frontier fighting begins. Some of the great lords are also secret allies of Hungarian and Polish nobles through marriage, which allows them to choose the side that will benefit their own estates if war breaks out.
krakow:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Duchy of Krakow and Sandomierz spans the middle Vistula plain and the highlands of Lesser Poland. Its center is the Wawel castle, built on a limestone cliff in a bend of the Vistula, and the busy city of Krakow below it. Its walls follow the rock face, and the cathedral inside the castle is where the Polish kings have been crowned and buried. Wheat fields and forest alternate across the fertile plain. Wooden barges carry grain and timber down the Vistula to the Baltic market at Gdansk. The Wieliczka salt mines, among the largest salt deposits in Europe, lie inside the duchy and make Lesser Poland the economic heart of the Piast lands. Copper caravans from Hungary also cross the Carpathian passes, and their trade feeds the towns along the river. Each spring the river floods the meadows, and herdsmen drive their cattle to higher ground until the water recedes.

Legitimacy and the crown. Duke Boleslaw V the Chaste holds Wawel and enjoys the honorary primacy of the Polish princes. His title rests on Piast descent and on the old custom that the senior duke sits at Krakow. Court judges and bishops decide legal cases together, and royal chancery documents are still written in Latin and open with the words 'In the name of God.' Each Easter the lesser princes come to the great hall of Wawel and kiss the duke's hand to confirm his seniority. Central royal power has broken apart since the Mongols destroyed the main Polish knightly host at Legnica in 1241. The realm is now a set of princely fragments, each pursuing its own interests, and the duke's orders are obeyed only within his own household and the towns that pay him. His core aim is to restore the Piast seniority so that the other branches again acknowledge Krakow as the first among them, and to make Church lands answer to royal courts once more.

Taxation and the salt economy. The duchy's income depends on the lease of the Wieliczka mines and on customs from the copper merchants who cross the Carpathian passes. Most of this income is taken by greedy barons and bishops. Barons set up their own toll posts on their estates, and bishops exempt church estates from tax in the name of their dioceses, so the duke's treasury receives far less than the mines produce. The steward's reports show rising output each year, yet the ducal accounts show less coin than before. The gap is covered by loans from Jewish moneylenders in Krakow and by pledges of salt tithes to the bishops. Every year the duke must also pay an annuity to the Silesian princes to keep them from raiding the border. The sum is renegotiated each year, and when talks fail, payments are delayed and the court budget cannot be set on time.

Military system. The Polish army follows the Western tradition of heavy cavalry charges. Knights wear mail and early plate, value personal courage and fight with lances. The army has no central command. Each lord brings his own retinue to the muster, and the retinues seldom march together. Against fast raiders who attack from unexpected directions, or against Lithuanian ambushes in the forest, the knights often charge before the infantry has formed, and their formation breaks as soon as they meet the enemy's first volley. The infantry is mostly drawn from city tradesmen and serfs. They are untrained and armed with spears and pitchforks. Castle walls are strong, but the garrisons are small, and a gate may be held by only a few dozen men.

Geopolitical crisis. The external threat is severe. Lithuanian raiders cross the Bug almost every year to burn villages and take captives, and their booty stretches as far as the Sandomierz border. Hungary's Arpad dynasty presses the southern border with political pressure and demands concessions on trade and marriage. The most dangerous sign is the gathering of a second major Mongol invasion from the Golden Horde on the eastern horizon. Scouts report Tatar patrols in the Ruthenian marches, and the border garrisons have been ordered to watch the fords. An invasion from the east would reach Krakow through the same river valleys that the Mongols used in 1241.

Internal factions. The dukes of Mazovia and the princes of Silesia each claim the seniority of Krakow for themselves. Local nobles use their veto in the assemblies to block the duke's decisions, and each veto delays the realm's response for another season. The Church plays its own game. Bishops refuse to pay for the army unless their privileges are confirmed, and some of them have appealed to Rome against royal seizures of church property. As a result the duke cannot raise a full royal guard even when the realm faces invasion, and each lord is left to defend his own fields.
prussia:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Prussian tribal confederation lives in the Baltic forests, marshes and coastal lagoons between the Vistula and the Neman. The land is broken and remote. Peat bogs, glacial hills and dense primeval forests form a natural maze that is hard for outsiders to cross. Settlements sit on the high ground above lakes and river bends, and each one is ringed by timber palisades and earthen banks. The Vistula lagoon and the coastal dunes provide fish, salt and amber. Herbs, wild honey and furs come from the forest, and amber crafts are made in the villages. Good farmland is scarce, so rye and oats are grown in forest clearings and yield little. Each spring the flooded bogs force families to move camp by canoe along the waterways, and they return to the hills before winter.

Legitimacy and the sacred order. The tribes are organized by clan and blood ties. Each clan worships the spirits of nature and ancient gods such as Perkunas. The sacred groves are presided over by the priest Krive, who holds the sacred staff and settles disputes and oaths between clans. A man who breaks an oath sworn in the grove loses his place in the clan, and the kin of the wronged party may hunt him down. Marriage, inheritance and the division of spoils follow old custom and require clan assembly approval. Every winter solstice the clans light fires in the grove and offer horses, honey and furs to ask for a good hunt in the coming year. The chiefs come from the oldest clans, and their authority depends on their control of the grove and its sacred objects. The priest keeps the tribes' old songs and the formulas of the blood oath. New oaths are spoken under the grove's oak, and every clan member witnesses them. Under the Order's pressure the priests disagree about what the gods require, and this disagreement shapes the choices each clan makes.

Taxation and tribute. The tribes have no taxes in the Western sense. Each clan gives a share of its hunt, honey and furs to the grove at harvest, and the priests redistribute these goods to the families who lost a man in war. Grain is scarce, so clans trade amber for salt and grain brought from the Baltic coast. A clan that refuses to bring its share to the grove is shunned until it pays. Trading points are set at river mouths and lakeshores, and outside merchants must first offer a gift to the priest before they may trade within tribal lands. Amber moves south along the old coastal road, and the tribes that hold its river crossings keep a portion of each load as payment for safe passage.

Military system. Prussian warriors are tall and fearless. They fight barefoot in knee-deep bog and carry barbed javelins, wooden shields covered with thick hide, and heavy curved swords. Their tactics favor ambush and feigned retreat into soft swamp ground, where they close in and cut down or drown armored knights who have fallen from their horses. Bows are short and light, with limited range. No standing army exists. Each clan sends men as needed, and these men train as hunters in peacetime. Before a campaign, warriors fast for three days in the sacred grove and rub herbs on their bodies, which they believe protects them from cold water. A warrior who survives a battle without fighting hand to hand is considered unfinished and must prove his courage again before he may marry.

Geopolitical crisis. The tribes face the threat of destruction. The Teutonic Order has driven brick crusader castles into their homeland like nails. Every winter the Order's knights burn villages, force baptism and reduce those who refuse to serfdom owing labor and tithes. Each new castle takes the best hunting grounds of a clan and turns them into fields for German settlers who arrive with plows and charters. Lithuanian riders also cross the Neman from the east and carry off cattle and honey. The southern border is now cut by Order castles, and the old roads to the amber coast are blocked, so the tribes can no longer trade for iron and salt. When Order wagons were ambushed in the forest, some clans shared the seized grain with starving villagers. This won them respect in some villages and invited Order reprisals.

Internal factions. The confederation has no central government and no unified army. In peacetime the clans fight over hunting grounds and sacred springs. Later accounts remember the Prussian uprising leader Herkus Monte as a hostage educated in Magdeburg. In 1259, however, he should not be presented as already organizing a region-wide rising. The tribes may resent the Order's levies and land seizure, while any wider alliance remains uncertain. Older elders doubt that the clans can unite. Some have quietly accepted the Order's offers of safe conduct and land in return for baptism, and others refuse to ally with clans that have made peace with the Order. The priests also disagree about the sacrifice that the grove requires. The old priests want the ancient rite and the sacrifice of captives, while the younger priests want to fight rather than offer prisoners to the grove. The contacts show alliance was discussed, but the tribes remained divided; no source places a region-wide rising under his leadership in 1259.
baltic_tribes:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Baltic tribes are mainly the Samogitians, the Curonians and the Jotvingians. They hold the forests between the southeastern Baltic coast and the western reaches of Lithuania. Much of the land is almost impassable to armies. Quicksand and bottomless bogs, which local people call kurms, lie between dense woods. The tribal economy rests on hunting in the undergrowth, beekeeping, fishing along the coast and raiding passing caravans. Amber is the only hard currency. Fishing villages line the dunes, and their families gather amber from the sand after the storms. They trade it to outsiders for iron weapons and salt, and the richest households keep their amber in clay jars under the hearth. Wooden walkways and portage trails link the villages on the lake shores, and in spring the river crossings often wash out and must be rebuilt.

Legitimacy and the sacred order. Each tribe is ruled by hereditary elders and by shamans who lead the rites. The elders hold the land and the spoils, and the shamans read omens before any campaign. A leader must win the shamans' approval at the sacred oak assembly before he can declare war or make peace. The tribes practice a strict blood feud. A killing must be answered by the killing of a member of the offender's kin within a year, or the whole clan loses its right to marry outside. Missionaries are not welcome. One priest who set up a wooden cross in a village was found dead on a forest path the next morning, and the villagers burned the cross as firewood. At the spring and autumn assemblies the clans decide on war, peace and the division of the spoils. The rule is that the clan that first offers a wild animal at the oak takes its share first, and the shamans settle disputes by divination.

Taxation and the spoils economy. The tribes do not levy taxes in the Western sense. Their wealth comes from spoils, captives and livestock taken in raids. Captives work as laborers in the longhouses, and the war leader divides the spoils by a fixed share among the families who took part. Disputes over these shares have caused some of the deepest feuds in the forest, because a warrior who thinks he was cheated will claim what he is owed from the other clan. Amber is weighed in front of the elders, and any person caught hiding amber is expelled from the clan.

Military system. The warriors are among the most feared forest hunters of eastern Europe. They carry short bows whose arrows are smeared with a poisonous paste, light javelins that pierce mail, and long-handled axes. They attack marching columns in blizzards or thick fog and vanish before the enemy can respond. They usually set ambushes in the trees beside a forest road and throw javelins from all sides once the column enters a narrow track. They avoid open battle and prefer to wear down an enemy by cutting supply lines, using wooden barriers and smoke to stop cavalry. Their weakness is logistics. A campaign longer than about ten days exhausts their food and arrows, and the warriors must return to the forest. Adult men learn archery and foot travel, and each clan keeps a band of young javelin men who guard the hunting grounds and lead the army's advance in war. Javelin tips are dipped in pine resin mixed with herbs, so even a scratch can cause a high fever.

Geopolitical crisis. The tribes are squeezed from both sides. The Livonian Order of the Sword holds the northern lands, and the Teutonic Order holds the south. Each border becomes a line of stone castles that must be crossed or avoided. Order scouts burn the beehives on the forest edge in spring, which cuts the honey harvest sharply. Lithuanian riders cross the Neman from the east and carry off livestock and people. The amber road is closed, and the tribes can no longer trade for iron. Several clans have had their camps burned twice in a single year, and they have fled to the bogs, where they survive on peat and bark. The Order's loggers have cut into the sacred oak groves, which the elders regard as sacrilege. At the spring assembly some may call for greater offerings of livestock or honey and renewed defense oaths; human sacrifice should not be presented as a documented local rite.

Internal factions. The clans have deep quarrels over spoils and who leads their rites. Some have made a private truce with the Order, accepting its protection of their hunting grounds in exchange for a share of their amber. Other clans see this as betrayal and want to punish the truce-makers under the blood-feud rule. Older shamans call for traditional offerings and protection rites, while younger leaders argue that the clans should answer encroachment through common defense. They disagree over how ritual and resistance should be ordered. The tribes also lack a common army for a long campaign, and each elder must choose between fighting to the end, submitting to the Teutonic castles or being absorbed into the Lithuanian grand duchy. This choice could split the tribes apart. If the oath assembly fails, the clans will fight alone, and the Order can defeat them one at a time.
tver:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Principality of Tver sits where the upper Volga meets the Tvertsa. The land is open and flat, and the river banks are fertile. Boats crowd the river throughout the navigation season, and the towns along the banks handle the grain and timber moving from the Volga basin toward Novgorod. The town of Tver has oak palisades and deep ditches, and its wooden churches and the prince's residence stand on opposite banks of the river. Fields on the river terraces grow rye, oats and flax. Flax is beaten and woven into coarse linen, which is sold in Novgorod and Lower Novgorod markets. Spring floods drown the low villages each year, so farmers keep their grain stores on raised platforms. The northern forests produce sable and pine resin, and hunters carry their pelts to the town, where the prince's clerks inspect each one and seal it with lead.

Legitimacy and the crown. The principality belongs to a branch of the Rurik family. Prince Yaroslav Yaroslavich, brother of Grand Prince Alexander Nevsky, considers himself the strongest heir to the grand princely title of Vladimir. He competes with his brother Alexander and other Rurikid princes for leadership in the northeast. His court sends letters and gifts to the Saray camp to remind the khan of Tver's loyalty, and each new embassy carries a list of gifts and promises of tribute. The khan's yarlyk goes to the prince who can offer the most silver, so the principality's diplomacy is mostly a contest of payments. The prince's court applies the old Rurikid custom. Local disputes are judged by the prince's officers together with the parish priests, and princely decrees are read aloud in church after the liturgy. His central aims are to win the khan's recognition as grand prince, to control the Volga-Novgorod river route, and to make Tver the political center of the northeast.

Taxation and the river economy. Control of the transit point between the Volga and Novgorod brings Tver large customs revenue and river tolls. Every boat that passes the town pays a fee in silver or pelts, and the prince's officers collect it at the landing stages. Unpaid cargoes are held in port until the debt is cleared. Dues are also charged on cloth, salt and honey sold in the town market, and a weigher appointed by the prince checks each sale. The prince's officers also collect grain taxes and labor service from nearby villages, and in winter peasants must cut and haul timber for the prince's court. When the khan demands more tribute, the prince raises the transit duty, and merchants often respond by taking their boats down the Lower Novgorod route. Each shift in traffic changes the revenue almost at once.

Military system. The army is built around heavy boyar cavalry in mail with long broadswords. Each boyar brings armored retainers to the field, and the professional household troops, the druzhina, are paid each quarter from the river customs. The principality is skilled in pontoon bridges and can ferry troops across the Volga and the Tvertsa within days. Its warriors fight hard in close combat, and the defense of fortified towns is a specialty. The treasury can keep professional soldiers paid through long campaigns, which is rare in the northeast. Horses are bought from the steppe edge, and their price rises sharply in wartime. Each campaign thus raises the principality's expenses. Supplies depend on the river, so a frozen or blocked waterway can stop an expedition and force the prince to turn back.

Geopolitical crisis. The chief contest is over the khan's yarlyk and the title of grand prince. Tver seeks support among other Rus princes and in Novgorod, hoping that a change at the Saray court may open a path to the title. An independent Moscow principality was not yet a rival in 1259, so later border conflicts with Moscow should not be projected back into this opening. The immediate uncertainty is whether the khan will recognize Yaroslav or a competing prince.

Internal factions. The prince's drive for centralized rule and the wartime levy has angered the old boyar families. These great landholders now hold private meetings. Some want a council that would limit the prince's power, while others want the household troops disbanded and the river revenue shared among the old families. Their resentment could become a conspiracy that paralyzes the state at the moment it needs to act. The household troops are paid from the river tolls, so any drop in boat traffic on the Volga would at once threaten the prince's ability to pay them. Some boyar retainers have been sent to the frontier and then stalled on the road, demanding food from villages along the way, which slows every campaign and sharpens the quarrel with the court.
smolensk:
Geography and economic lifeblood. The Principality of Smolensk sits on high, steep hills above the upper Dnieper, where roads from the Baltic, the Black Sea and the Moscow river basin meet. The city lies on the south bank of the river and is protected by deep ditches, earth ramparts and tall timber towers. The high ground favors the defenders and makes any assault costly. Forests around the city supply timber, furs and honey, and iron workshops along the river turn local ore into tools and weapons. Timber rafts float down the Dnieper toward Kyiv and the Black Sea. Cropland lies in the valley bottoms, where the soil is heavy and suited to oats and flax. Spring floods force villages to move to higher ground until the water recedes.

Legitimacy and the crown. Smolensk is one of the oldest Rurikid principalities in Rus. Its princes take pride in their pure blood and in the law code Russkaya Pravda, which the city's courts still apply. The bishop and the boyar council check the prince's power closely. Court cases follow the code, and fines are set by the status of the injured party, so the penalties for nobles and commoners differ. A prince who wishes to make war or sign a treaty must win the consent of the council in the cathedral square, and the bishop must bless the oath. The seals of the princely chancery are kept by the bishop, and every important charter requires both seals. Grand Prince Gleb Rostislavich rules by this arrangement. His central aims are to keep the principality independent, to bring the Dnieper towns under his authority, and to protect the river route that makes Smolensk rich.

Taxation and the river economy. The treasury depends on tolls along the Varangian-to-Greek water route, on iron workshops and on exports of timber and furs from the surrounding forests. Merchants from Smolensk carry wax, honey and hides down the Dnieper to the Black Sea markets, and they return with salt, wine and cloth. Each boat that passes the city landing pays a toll set by the weight and value of its cargo. Furs and honey carry higher rates than coarse cloth. Foresters and hunters pay a tenth of their catch to the prince's officers. River tolls are the largest single source of revenue, and the council watches the tollhouses closely. When spring floods or summer drought block the river, customs income drops and the treasury must borrow from wealthy boyars to pay the garrison.

Military system. The army is known for its heavy infantry. Foot soldiers carry shields as tall as a man and double-edged crescent axes. They form iron-wall blocks that can stop a cavalry charge head on. In siege fighting these blocks are very hard to dislodge, and each fortress garrison is drilled to hold its walls until relief arrives. The weakness is the lack of fast light cavalry. Garrisons keep stores of dry timber and stone-throwing ammunition for the gates, since a winter siege is the most common way a fortress falls. In open battle the army can be kited and worn down by enemy horse archers who keep their distance and shoot. Armor is in short supply. Many new recruits fight in leather jackets because the armorers cannot make enough mail for every man.

Geopolitical crisis. The most serious threat is the steady infiltration of Lithuanian forest cavalry from the west. Several border forts have already fallen to dawn attacks. Each lost fort opens a new road into the principality, and Lithuanian riders use those roads to raid the villages along the Dnieper. The border garrisons are small, enough to hold off a raid but not a planned siege. Reinforcements take weeks to arrive, and by the time they come the Lithuanian horsemen have withdrawn, leaving burned villages behind them. Trade routes through Vitebsk have shrunk, so salt and iron are harder to obtain. Grand Prince Gleb also pays regular tribute to the Golden Horde, which has drawn the attention of the khan's envoys to the river trade.

Internal factions. The court is split between conservative boyars who oppose tribute and pragmatic officials who want peace with the khan. Zealous clergy and their followers among the common people condemn the prince for paying the Tatars, and sermons in the cathedral have become political speeches. The three factions, which are the anti-tribute boyars, the pro-tribute officials and the clerical critics, deadlock the boyar council, and each session ends without a decision. The townsmen divide along similar lines. Craftsmen tend to support the anti-tribute party, and merchants fear that a break with the khan would close the river. Any outside attack could turn this divided principality into a state out of control and cost it the Dnieper gateway. The bishop has also threatened to excommunicate any boyar who sells land to the khan's tax collectors, which gives the Church leverage in every quarrel over tribute.
